name: Nikhil Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or political groups. This is confidential. Tell me about an ordinary day on your building site.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am the senior carpenter on a small building crew, mostly framing and repair work where an old doorway has to take a new door. I have a vocational trade certificate and am usually the one handing an apprentice the tape before the saw. I'm fifty-eight, with my partner, grown children and a retirement date we hope our wages can support; we have a few months of expenses saved. My pay is ordinary for this work and there are some other builders nearby, but I would rather earn by finishing a sound job than spend evenings learning a screen I have never needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI Plateau sounds like office paper moving faster while carpenters still fit the frames. A builder can print a straight line, but an old doorway is seldom square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I would be relieved, because I want several more years on a normal wage before I slow down. A few months saved is useful, yet one stopped site could still upset our retirement sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep leading framing and repair shifts and add a small amount from each full wage to our savings when bills permit. In the first year after this modest change, I'd keep measuring by hand and ask the builder about the next paid site before this one ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than calm, since the work itself looks safe but the next contract is not promised. I know there are some builders nearby, though changing crews at my age takes effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you teach an apprentice at an old doorway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the top and bottom of the opening and mark the narrower number. The last apprentice learned that lesson when a new door caught on old plaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you add to savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would put in the extra savings only after regular bills are covered. We want a real balance, not a number written into a hopeful retirement plan.

say: **AI Plateau** would leave physical framing and repairs in carpenters’ hands.
I would tell the crew a printed **straight line** cannot make an old doorway square.
think: I need several more **normal wage years** before our planned slowdown.
Our **few months saved** will not cover a long gap between building sites.
do: **Keep** leading framing shifts and measuring doorways by hand.
**Add** from full wages to household savings only when bills permit.
**Ask** the builder about the next paid site before current work ends.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about ordinary site gaps even though AI adds little new pressure.
S0.quote: A builder can print a straight line, but an old doorway is seldom square.
fieldNote: His **traditional trade pride** focuses on measuring a real opening before cutting.
Moderate savings and **ordinary pay** keep contract gaps on his mind despite several possible nearby builders.

steps.text: Keep leading framing shifts and measuring old doorways by hand
Add from full wages to household savings only after bills permit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Steady Disruption will reach the builder's ordering and bookings before a robot fits our doors. I would ask whoever sets a new target to carry the wrong materials back themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faster office could schedule fewer paid days for the crew, and I might be one of the older hands told to stay home. I will not claim the new plan means a lost job, but one day less a week would hurt our savings target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep doing paid repair shifts and ask for next month's rota in writing. In the first year I'd compare the new material orders with hand measurements, and apply to a posted local carpentry job if our paid days fell for two months and its wage covered our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing a day, irritated by the idea that speed on a screen equals care on site. I could look at another builder, but I would rather keep this crew if the pay holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check whether hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count the paid days on the new rota against the last two months. A new title would mean nothing if the payslip had fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another builder worth applying to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply only after seeing a real local posting with safe work and enough pay. I am not leaving a current wage for a builder's rumour.

say: **Steady Disruption** would change orders and bookings before physical repair carpentry.
I would ask management to own **wrong materials** and show the crew its paid rota.
think: A shorter **paid week** could cut our savings before retirement.
I might be the **older carpenter** sent home first, though that is a worry rather than a certainty.
do: **Keep** paid repair shifts and compare new orders with hand measurements.
**Request** next month’s paid rota and compare it with the previous two months.
**Apply** to a posted local carpentry job only after two shorter months at safe, bill-covering pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost paid days, though another nearby builder is an option.
S1.quote: A new title would mean nothing if the payslip had fewer hours.
fieldNote: He rejects **screen-led targets** but does not assume the new plan has already cost his job.
His **job application** requires two months of lower paid days plus a posted local safe role at enough pay.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and compare new material orders with hand measurements
Apply after two shorter months to posted safe local carpentry job only at bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2028 could write the plans and order materials almost at once, with capable hands-on building robots around 2031. A robot cannot go onto our site without someone responsible for stopping it safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty when thinking work changes, and robots three years later could take the repair shifts I count on. A few months of savings would not carry my partner and me to the retirement date we hope for, so the thought keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd request a paid supervised robot-safety trial from the builder, and take practical building-maintenance training only if a recognised place is offered with funded fees and paid time. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep repair shifts, check AI drawings against real openings, and apply after that training for posted local school-maintenance work only if its pay covers our household bills and duties are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, to be plain. I have a plan on paper, but the fast robot date could remove the wage before we have enough saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a robot trial safe enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trial would need a fenced work area and a stop control a carpenter can reach. If the builder offers no paid supervised place, I will not pretend I have tested a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in a maintenance posting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the school for its posted wage, hours and actual repair duties before applying. A maintenance certificate would not pay the food bill without a real local vacancy.

say: **AGI by 2028** would change plans first, with capable site robots around 2031.
I would require a **reachable stop control** before any robot entered our building site.
think: I could lose **repair wages** before our planned retirement budget is ready.
A few months of **savings** will not cover the years between a lost job and that target.
do: **Request** a paid supervised robot-safety trial with fenced space and reachable stop control.
**Take** recognised practical maintenance training only with offered place, funded fees and paid time.
**Apply** after training to posted local school-maintenance work only with safe duties and bill-covering pay.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because I expect a serious wage loss and cannot bridge years with our reserve.
S2.quote: A maintenance certificate would not pay the food bill without a real local vacancy.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 paperwork** from the possible 2031 replacement of physical repair hours.
His **trial request** is not a test performed; training and job application each require funded, paid or posted conditions.

steps.text: Take recognised maintenance course only with funded fees paid time and offered place
Apply after training for posted safe local school-maintenance job only at bill-covering pay
Keep paid repairs and check AI drawings against real openings
Request paid supervised robot trial with fenced space and reachable stop control

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives five years before the plans change and until around 2034 before robots can match site hands. I would use those years to earn, save and make sure an apprentice can still read a tape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three I may be close to leaving full-time carpentry. I cannot set a retirement date by age alone. If savings and available retirement income fall short, I will need paid work, whether on this crew or at a local maintenance job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd add to savings from full paid weeks and take a recognised practical building-maintenance course only if the builder offers a place with funded fees and paid time. In the first year after 2031, I'd keep carpentry shifts while available and apply after that training to a posted local school-maintenance vacancy only if the wage covers bills and the duties fit my knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because extra years help but do not promise the money we need. I can prepare without pretending I have already been hired elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which maintenance duties would be safe for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the stair work, lifting and callout hours in the school posting. If the duties would damage my knees, the wage would not make it a safe move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you settle the leaving date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would add up actual savings, wages and any retirement income then available. We would move the date if the money did not cover ordinary living costs.

say: **AGI by 2031** gives more earning time before capable building robots arrive around 2034.
I would keep teaching **tape work** while checking a paid maintenance route.
think: Age **sixty-three** does not guarantee we can live without carpentry wages.
A **local maintenance job** helps only after paid funded training and a safe posted role at enough pay.
do: **Add** savings from full paid carpentry weeks while bills allow.
**Take** recognised maintenance training only with funded fees, paid time and an offered place.
**Apply** after training to posted local school-maintenance work only with safe duties and bill-covering wages.
feel: I feel **anxious** about an uncertain retirement budget, though the longer runway lets me prepare.
S3.quote: I cannot set a retirement date by age alone.
fieldNote: He will not treat **2031** as an automatic retirement date or a guaranteed pension.
The **maintenance move** is separate from course completion and hinges on a posted local safe job with adequate wages.

steps.text: Add to savings from full paid carpentry weeks when bills permit
Take recognised maintenance course only with funded fees paid time and offered place
Apply after training for posted safe local maintenance job only at bill-covering wages
Keep carpentry shifts after 2031 while paid site work remains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2036 leaves a decade before thinking AI changes plans and until around 2039 before capable building robots arrive. I would spend the years earning and teaching proper repairs, not guessing at the date of my last wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I might have stopped full-time work if wages, savings and our later budget line up. If we still need income after 2036, I would take safe part-time carpentry or maintenance shifts, but only where a real local opening pays enough to fill the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep paid framing and repair shifts and add a set amount to savings from full weeks if bills permit. In the first year after 2036, if our budget still needs a wage, I'd apply to a posted local part-time repair role only if the duties are safe for my knees and the pay covers the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the money even with ten years. A long warning gives us room to save, but the local builder still has to have paid work for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What repair skill would you pass on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach a younger carpenter to check a door frame at three heights before ordering. A bowed wall has made a fool of more than one confident drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you still need wages after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would write the income gap on paper after counting actual savings and any retirement payments available then. If the gap is zero, I can leave the paid rota; if not, I need a posted safe job, not a promise.

say: **AGI by 2036** gives a decade before plan work changes and longer before capable site robots.
I would keep **teaching repairs** while earning rather than assume an exact retirement date.
think: Our **full-time exit** depends on actual wages, savings and later available retirement income.
If a **budget gap** remains after 2036, safe paid local repair work is necessary.
do: **Keep** paid framing shifts and teach door-frame checks to younger carpenters.
**Add** a set amount to savings from full paid weeks only if bills permit.
**Apply** after 2036 for posted safe local part-time repairs only if wages fill our budget gap.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because ten years of warning cannot guarantee paid work or enough savings.
S4.quote: A bowed wall has made a fool of more than one confident drawing.
fieldNote: He values **apprentice teaching** and keeps saving from actual full paid weeks, not assumed future income.
Later **part-time work** remains conditional on a household gap, a posted local opening and safe duties at adequate pay.

steps.text: Keep paid framing shifts and teach door-frame checks to younger carpenters
Add to savings from full paid weeks only if bills permit
Apply after 2036 for posted safe local part-time repairs only if wages fill gap

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because plans could change before the crew is ready and capable robots around 2031 could take the repair wage we need. A paid supervised safety trial, funded practical training with paid time and a posted local maintenance job at safe, bill-covering wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who pays when a robot's bad cut ruins a wall. The carpenter should not lose a paid day because an untested machine spoiled the job.

portrait: **Nikhil**, fifty-eight, leads framing and repairs on building sites after earning a vocational trade certificate.
He has **typical trade pay**, a partner, grown children, only a few months saved and some other nearby builders.
He **avoids new technology**, never uses AI, and trusts apprenticeships and measured work more than unproven screens.
The **2028** case threatens wages before his hoped-for retirement; longer warnings let him save and consider paid practical maintenance training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change plans quickly and bring capable building robots around 2031, threatening his needed repair wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid safety trial**, funded practical training with paid time and a posted safe local maintenance role at bill-covering wages would help.
headlineQuote: The carpenter should not lose a paid day because an untested machine spoiled the job.
